name: Disana
description: Germany. Founded 1969. Oldest organic textile brand. Fine knit + boiled wool. Also organic cotton cloth nappies + wool diaper covers. All made in Germany.

name: Engel Natur
description: Germany (family business since 1927). Merino/silk base layers. Babies through adults. No chemical finishing. No AZO dyes.

name: Reiff Strickmode
description: Germany. 100% wool fleece specialist. Baby sleep sacks in multiple weights (1.0, 2.5, 3.5 TOG). Made in-house.

name: Hocosa
description: Switzerland. Wool/silk/cotton underwear and outerwear. Organic kbT animal husbandry.

name: Pure Pure by Bauer
description: Germany/Italy. 100% natural fibre. Gender-open baby clothes. Hats, mittens, rompers, cardigans.

name: Nui Organics
description: New Zealand. Organic Merino wool + cotton. Temperature-regulating. Popular in Waldorf homes globally.

name: ⭐ SteinerBooks / Anthroposophic Press (USA)
description: The primary USA publisher and bookshop for Steiner's works and all anthroposophical books. Full catalogue, digital editions, new releases. steinerbooks.org · Also: rudolfsteinerbookstore.com

name: ⭐ Waldorf Publications (USA)
description: AWSNA's publishing arm. Curriculum guides, teacher resources, research and parent books. Full catalogue and online store. waldorfpublications.org

name: ⭐ Floris Books (UK/International)
description: Scotland, UK. One of the world's most important Waldorf publishers — Steiner's works, child development, education, biodynamics, children's books. Ships internationally. florisbooks.co.uk

name: Hawthorn Press (UK/International)
description: UK. Specialists in Waldorf education, arts and crafts, family life and social renewal. Many of the most-read Waldorf parenting books. hawthornpress.com · Ships internationally.

name: WECAN Books (USA)
description: Waldorf Early Childhood Association of North America. Publisher of early childhood books, songbooks and curriculum resources. waldorfearlychildhood.org/store

name: rsarchive.org (Free)
description: All of Steiner's education lectures available free online. The Education of the Child, Study of Man, Kingdom of Childhood and 6,000+ other lectures. Free. Always check here before buying.

name: 🫀 Fundamentals of Therapy
description: Rudolf Steiner & Ita Wegman. Foundational text of anthroposophic medicine. How to think about health, illness and healing from conception onward. Essential for parents and practitioners.

name: 🫀 Cradle of a Healthy Life
description: Dr. Johanna Steegmans. WECAN. Pregnancy, birth and the first weeks through an anthroposophical lens. Physical and spiritual preparation for the child's arrival.

name: 🫀 Conception, Birth and Early Childhood
description: Norbert Glas. SteinerBooks. Anthroposophical view of conception, prenatal life and birth. The physical and spiritual significance of these first moments.

name: 💛 A Warm and Gentle Welcome
description: Margaret Ris & Trice Atchison. WECAN. Nurturing children from birth to age three. Welcoming the new soul into family life with warmth, rhythm and simplicity.

name: 🫀 The Child from Birth to Three in Waldorf Education
description: Patzlaff, Grah-Wittich & Howard (eds). WECAN. Physical, emotional and spiritual development in the first three years. Concrete suggestions for home and care settings.

name: 🫀 The First Three Years of the Child
description: Karl König. SteinerBooks. Walking, speaking, thinking — the three great developmental achievements. Written by the founder of Camphill. Deep, beautiful, essential.

name: 🫀 Raising Sound Sleepers
description: Dr. Adam Blanning MD. SteinerBooks (2024). Helping infants and young children develop healthy sleep through sensory awareness and rhythm. Anthroposophic family medicine.

name: 🫀 A Waldorf Guide to Children's Health
description: Dr. Michaela Glöckler, Dr. Wolfgang Goebel & Dr. Karin Michael. Floris. Essential family health reference from birth through adolescence. Illnesses, symptoms, anthroposophic treatments. The Waldorf family's household medical book.

name: 💛 The Dignity of the Young Child
description: Dr. Michaela Glöckler. WECAN. Care for the first three years. The inner life and dignity of the infant and what babies truly need from adults.

name: 💛 The Creative Word
description: Daniel Udo de Haes. WECAN. The young child's experience of language and storytelling. How speech forms the soul of the very young child in the first years.

name: ☀️ Creative Play for Your Baby
description: Christopher Clouder & Janni Nicol. Hawthorn. Open-ended, age-appropriate play from birth. Natural toys, sensory play, Waldorf-informed developmental activities for 0–2 years.

name: ☀️ Nurturing Children and Families
description: Sarah Baldwin. WECAN. One model of a parent-child programme in a Waldorf school. Songs, movement, seasonal crafts and rhythm for babies and toddlers.

name: The Care and Development of the Human Senses
description: Willi Aeppli. Steiner Schools Fellowship. Significance of the twelve senses in early childhood education. How sense experiences shape healthy physical development.

name: The First Seven Years: Physiology of Childhood
description: Edmond Schoorel (Netherlands). RSC Press. What is happening in the young child's body during the first seven years — the etheric body and its work. Landmark physiological text.

name: The Twelve Senses
description: Albert Soesman (Netherlands). Hawthorn. Touch, life, self-movement, balance, smell, taste, sight, warmth, hearing, language, concept, ego — clearly explained. Why foundational senses matter for learning and health.

name: Under the Sky
description: Sally Schweizer (UK). Sophia Books. Playing, working and enjoying in the open air. The outdoor Waldorf life — mud, water, seasons, physical exploration. Movement as medicine for the developing body.

name: You Are Your Child's First Teacher
description: Rahima Baldwin Dancy (USA). THE gateway book for all Waldorf parents. Practical, warm, comprehensive. Covers imitation, rhythm, temperament, play, sleep, discipline, festivals, media. Birth to age 7 primarily.

name: Beyond the Rainbow Bridge
description: Barbara Patterson & Pamela Bradley (USA). Michaelmas Press. Nurturing children from birth to seven. Rhythm, will forces, temperament, and how environment shapes the young child's soul.

name: Seven Times the Sun
description: Shea Darian (USA). Gilead Press. Guiding your child through the rhythms of the day. Songs, verses and daily rituals that create emotional security and seasonal rhythm in family life.

name: Simplicity Parenting
description: Kim John Payne (Australia/USA). Four steps: simplify environment, establish rhythm, schedule a break in schedules, filter the adult world. Reduces cumulative stress. The most widely read Waldorf-adjacent parenting book worldwide.

name: Healing Stories for Challenging Behaviour
description: Susan Perrow (Australia). Custom therapeutic stories using metaphor, journey and resolution to address specific behaviours — non-confrontationally. Translated into 10+ languages. Works from age 3 upward.

name: Nøkken: A Danish Waldorf Child Care
description: Helle Heckmann (Denmark). WECAN. Waldorf-inspired childminding. Community, rhythm, outdoor life. Emotional security through simple, unhurried daily life. Pioneer of the forest kindergarten movement.

name: Working with Anxious, Nervous and Depressed Children
description: Henning Köhler (Germany). Understanding children with emotional difficulties from an anthroposophic perspective. Practical tools for parents and teachers from age 3 upward.

name: Phases of Childhood
description: Bernard Lievegoed (Netherlands). Floris. Growing in body, soul and spirit through all developmental phases. A classic anthroposophical developmental psychology spanning birth through adolescence.

name: Heaven on Earth
description: Sharifa Oppenheimer (USA). SteinerBooks. Creating the Waldorf kindergarten at home. Rhythm, play environments, outdoor spaces, sensory richness, festival celebrations. Practical and beautiful.

name: Free to Learn
description: Lynne Oldfield (UK). Hawthorn. Introducing Steiner Waldorf early childhood education. The principles and methods of the kindergarten. Why childhood matters and early years should not be rushed.

name: The Genius of Play
description: Sally Jenkinson (UK). Hawthorn. Celebrating the spirit of childhood. The developmental necessity of unstructured, creative, imaginative play. A powerful case for protecting free play.

name: Work and Play in Early Childhood
description: Freya Jaffke (Germany). SteinerBooks. How meaningful domestic work — cooking, cleaning, gardening — forms the heart of the Waldorf kindergarten and builds the child's will forces.

name: On the Play of the Child
description: Freya Jaffke (ed) (Germany). WECAN. Steiner's indications for working with young children. Essential reading for kindergarten teachers and parents wanting to understand play more deeply.

name: Developmental Signatures (Ages 3–9)
description: Rainer Patzlaff et al. (Germany). AWSNA. Core values and practices in Waldorf education for children ages 3–9. Detailed developmental markers and how the kindergarten responds to them.

name: Understanding Children's Drawings
description: Michaela Strauss (Germany). Rudolf Steiner Press. Reading children's drawings as a developmental window. How a drawing reveals the child's inner developmental stage — invaluable for parents and teachers.

name: Creative Play for Your Toddler (Ages 2–4)
description: Christopher Clouder (UK). Hawthorn. Waldorf toy projects and age-appropriate sensory, movement and creative play for toddlers. Nature-based activities.

name: Gesture Games for Spring & Summer / Autumn & Winter
description: Wilma Ellersiek (Germany). WECAN. Finger games and seasonal gesture poems for kindergarten. Songs, movement, language and touch — deeply nourishing for the very young child developmentally.

name: Let Us Form a Ring / Dancing As We Sing
description: Nancy Foster (USA). WECAN. Circle games and songs for the kindergarten year. Movement and music woven together in seasonal rhythm.

name: Under the Stars
description: Renate Long-Breipohl (Australia/Germany). Hawthorn. Foundations of Steiner Waldorf early childhood education. International perspective — how these principles apply across cultures and countries.

name: First Grade Readiness
description: Nancy Blanning (ed). WECAN. Resources, insights and tools for navigating the transition from kindergarten to Grade 1. Key signs of physical, emotional and developmental readiness.

name: A Waldorf Guide to Children's Health (continued)
description: Glöckler, Goebel & Michael. Floris. Childhood illnesses, fevers, ear infections, common complaints throughout the school years. Why fever has developmental value. The household medical reference.

name: Educating Through Arts and Crafts
description: Michael Martin (ed) (UK). How handwork — knitting, weaving, carving, sewing — builds will forces, fine motor coordination and physical intelligence in the school-age child, Grades 1–8.

name: The Extra Lesson
description: Audrey McAllen (UK). Hawthorn. Movement-based remedial programme for reading, writing or arithmetic difficulties. Specific movement sequences that support brain integration. Grades 1–6.

name: Knit for Health and Wellness
description: Betsan Corkhill (UK). Research-based guide to knitting's measurable physical and mental health benefits. Used in Waldorf handwork teacher education and WHE conferences.

name: Crossing the Bridge: The Nine-Year Change
description: Hermann Koepke. SteinerBooks. A lucid, readable explanation of the 9-year threshold — why children suddenly feel alone and separate from parents and peers. What adults can do at this pivotal moment.

name: The Soul of Discipline
description: Kim John Payne (Australia/USA). Ballantine. Warm, firm and calm guidance from toddlers to teens. Developmentally appropriate discipline — how to respond differently at each age and stage.

name: Therapeutic Storytelling: 101 Healing Stories for Children
description: Susan Perrow (Australia). Hawthorn. 101 stories for challenging behaviour, grief, anxiety, bullying, teasing, nightmares, bedwetting and more. Ages 3–10+. Metaphor, journey and resolution framework.

name: An A-Z Collection of Behaviour Tales
description: Susan Perrow (Australia). Hawthorn. Illustrated quick-reference collection — from Angry Ant to Zestless Zebra. Find a story for a specific behavioural challenge instantly. Grades 1–4.

name: Stories to Light the Night
description: Susan Perrow (Australia). Hawthorn. Stories for grief, loss, death, divorce, adoption, pet loss, loss of health. 94 stories from multiple cultures. For when a child or class has experienced loss. Ages 5–adult.

name: A Practical Guide to Curative Education
description: Robyn M. Brown (USA). Lindisfarne Books, 440 pp. The seven life processes as a diagnostic and therapeutic lens for all children showing difficulties — for class teachers, parents and support staff Grades 1–8.

name: Being at Your Best When Your Kids Are at Their Worst
description: Kim John Payne (Australia/USA). Ballantine. How to regulate yourself in difficult parenting moments — staying grounded and present when the child is most challenging.

name: Storytelling with Children
description: Nancy Mellon (USA). Hawthorn. How to use story as the living heart of teaching across the grades. Fairy tales, nature stories, hero myths — why each type is right for each grade level.

name: Tasks and Content of the Steiner-Waldorf Curriculum
description: Rawson, Avison & Richter. Floris. Complete curriculum reference Grades 1–12. What is taught, why it is taught at that age, and how it relates to the child's development at each specific year.

name: A Handbook for Waldorf Class Teachers
description: Kevin Avison (UK). Floris. Comprehensive practical guide for class teachers. Grade-by-grade curriculum, teaching approaches and how to meet the developmental needs of each year from 1–8.

name: School as a Journey
description: Torin Finser (USA). SteinerBooks. An eight-year class teacher memoir — Grades 1–8 with one beloved class. The most inspiring account of what a Waldorf class teacher does year by year.

name: The Roadmap to Literacy
description: Janet Langley & Jennifer Militzer-Kopperl (USA). Mill City Press. Guide to teaching language arts in Waldorf schools, Grades 1–3. Phonics-based, developmentally appropriate, comprehensive. "Game changer."

name: Writing to Reading the Steiner Waldorf Way
description: Allanson & Teensma (UK). Floris. Foundations of creative literacy in Classes 1–2. How letters emerge from images and stories — the Waldorf approach to beginning reading and writing.

name: Making Math Meaningful: Grades 1–5
description: Fabrie, Gottenbos & Jamie York (Netherlands/USA). Step-by-step progressions, main lesson ideas, developmentally appropriate approach to all four processes in lower school.

name: Making Math Meaningful: Grades 6–8
description: Jamie York (USA). Middle school Waldorf math. Fractions, decimals, percents, geometry, algebra introduction — all with developmentally appropriate pacing and imaginative framing.

name: Creative Form Drawing
description: Ernst Schubert (Germany). Hawthorn. Form drawing for Classes 1–4. The Waldorf-specific subject that develops spatial sense, handwriting readiness, bilateral coordination and inner patterning.

name: Colouring with Block Crayons
description: Sieglinde de Francesca (USA). Floris. Classic guide to Waldorf block crayon technique — how colour is used developmentally in Grades 1–3 to nourish the feeling life through art.

name: Painting and Drawing in Waldorf Schools
description: Thomas Wildgruber (Germany). Floris. Definitive art curriculum guide — wet-on-wet painting, form drawing, charcoal and pastel from Grades 1–12 with full developmental rationale.

name: Waldorf Games Handbook
description: Kim John Payne, Waletzko & Garrett. Hawthorn. Circle games, seasonal games, singing games — movement-based learning for Grades 1–3 developing social skills and physical intelligence together.

name: 🫀 Making Math Meaningful: Grades 6–8
description: Jamie York (USA). Business math, irrational numbers, square roots, basic algebra, geometry — paced to the emerging capacity for abstract thinking in the pre-adolescent years.

name: 💛 The Soul of Discipline
description: Kim John Payne. The middle years — how to hold boundaries with warmth as the adolescent body and soul begins to emerge. Non-punitive approaches grounded in Waldorf development.

name: 💛 Therapeutic Storytelling
description: Susan Perrow (Australia). Stories for older children — grief, exclusion, anxiety, transition. The metaphor framework continues to work into early adolescence. Workshop training via susanperrow.com

name: ☀️ Tasks and Content of the Steiner-Waldorf Curriculum (Grades 6–8)
description: Rawson, Avison & Richter. Floris. Roman history, physics, chemistry, perspective drawing, world geography, algebra, biography — how each subject meets the 12–14 year old developmentally.

name: 🫀 A Waldorf Guide to Children's Health (adolescent chapters)
description: Glöckler, Goebel & Michael. Floris. Puberty, sleep, substance use, mental health — through an anthroposophic medical lens. Continues to be relevant through age 18.

name: 💛 Between Form and Freedom
description: Betty Staley (USA). Hawthorn. THE essential guide to adolescent development in Waldorf education. Identity, relationships, idealism, emotional volatility, the search for meaning. Required reading for high school teachers and parents of teenagers.

name: 💛 Education for Adolescents
description: Rudolf Steiner. SteinerBooks. The foundational text on the adolescent stage — how the ego forces work, what the young person needs from education. Used in Sunbridge and CfA high school programs.

name: 💛 Trailing Clouds of Glory
description: Douglas Gerwin (ed) (USA). Waldorf Publications. The changing relationships of young people through puberty and what teachers can do. Essays by multiple Waldorf high school educators.

name: ☀️ Making Math Meaningful: High School (Grades 9–12)
description: Jamie York (USA). 30 years of Waldorf high school math. Projective geometry, calculus, complex numbers, philosophy of math. "Chock-full of awe-inspiring mathematics."

name: ☀️ Education Towards Freedom
description: Frans Carlgren (Sweden). Floris. Beautifully illustrated international survey of Waldorf schools — covering kindergarten through high school. The iconic visual and narrative overview of the whole Waldorf journey.

name: ☀️ Understanding Waldorf Education
description: Jack Petrash (USA). Floris. Jargon-free. Kindergarten through high school from the inside out. Accessible and reassuring for parents of children in upper grades.

name: All Year Round
description: Druitt, Fynes-Clinton & Rowling (UK). Hawthorn. THE seasonal festival book — stories, crafts, recipes, songs for every season and festival. Suitable for all faiths and secular homes. Use from birth through high school.

name: Festivals Together
description: Fitzjohn, Weston & Large (UK). Hawthorn. A multicultural festival guide alongside the seasonal calendar. How to celebrate across faiths and cultures in the Waldorf spirit.

name: The Birthday Book
description: Ann Druitt & Christine Fynes-Clinton. Hawthorn. Waldorf-style birthday traditions, crafts and celebrations across ages. How to mark each year meaningfully as the child grows.

name: Making Peg Dolls & More
description: Margaret Bloom (UK). Hawthorn. Waldorf-inspired doll-making and craft projects for families. Seasonal nature crafts for children across age groups.

name: The Education of the Child
description: Rudolf Steiner. The foundational text. Every parent and teacher begins here. The three seven-year phases, the fourfold human being, how education must respond to child development.

name: Waldorf Education: Rudolf Steiner's Ideas in Practice
description: Christopher Clouder & Martyn Rawson (UK). Floris. Comprehensive overview from kindergarten through high school. Good for parents new to Waldorf at any stage.

name: Leaving Room for the Angels
description: Reg Down (Canada/SA/Ireland). AWSNA Publications. Eurythmy and the art of teaching. "The first section should be read by all Waldorf teachers." 240 pages. Artistic pedagogy through the lens of movement and eurythmy.

name: Education for Special Needs (Curative Education Course)
description: Rudolf Steiner. 12 lectures. Every curative educator begins here. Applicable across all age ranges. Free online at rsarchive.org; in print via Rudolf Steiner Press.

name: A Practical Guide to Curative Education
description: Robyn M. Brown. Lindisfarne Books, 440 pp. The seven life processes as a practical lens for all children — especially those with challenges. For class teachers, parents and support staff across all grade levels.

name: Children with a Difference
description: Walter Holtzapfel. Floris. Background of Steiner special education. How anthroposophical principles apply to various developmental and learning differences across childhood.

name: Autism: Medical, Educational and Social Issues
description: Karl König. Floris/SteinerBooks. Perspective on autism from the founder of Camphill. The spiritual individuality of autistic children — historic and still profoundly relevant.

name: 🇦🇷 Editorial Antroposófica (Argentina)
description: Primary Argentine publisher and bookshop. Full online store — Educación Waldorf, Medicina Antroposófica, Literatura Infantil, Pedagogía Curativa. Ships to all of Latin America. antroposofica.com.ar

name: 🇪🇸 Editorial Rudolf Steiner (Spain)
description: Founded 1975. The most complete Spanish-language publisher of Waldorf and Steiner books. Ships worldwide. editorialrudolfsteiner.com

name: 🇪🇸 Editorial Pau de Damasc (Spain)
description: Waldorf pedagogy, anthroposophy, Goethean science, curative education, children's stories in Spanish and Catalan. Also serves Chile (chile.paudedamasc.com). paudedamasc.com

name: 🇪🇸 ING Edicions (Spain)
description: Spanish Waldorf curriculum materials, art books, children's literature in Spanish. Pedagogía Waldorf section. ingedicions.com

name: 🇧🇷 Editora Antroposófica (Brazil)
description: Brazil's leading publisher for anthroposophical books in Portuguese. Full Waldorf pedagogy range. editora.com.br

description: Mexican bookshop distributing all major Spanish-language anthroposophical publishers: Antroposófica, Rudolf Steiner, Pau de Damasc, Idunn (Chile), Waldorf Publications and more. Ships to all of Latin America and Mexico.

name: 🌍 rsarchive.org (Free)
description: Rudolf Steiner Archive. Many Steiner lectures and foundational texts available free in Spanish online. Check before buying. rsarchive.org

name: 🌎 Revistas / Magazines
description: Campanada — Spanish-language Waldorf journal (revista) published by ING Edicions. The main ongoing Spanish-language Waldorf educational publication. · Erziehungskunst — some articles translated to Spanish. Search @erziehungskunst on Instagram for Spanish content.

name: Nanchen Natur
description: Germany. Handmade one-by-one. Each doll stuffed by hand with organic pure new wool. Each face individually hand-painted — no two alike. "Doll doctor" repair service. From 3 months+.

name: Ambrosius / Eco Flower Fairies
description: Romania / USA. Founded 1996 for the local Waldorf school in Cluj-Napoca. Wool felt flower fairies, gnomes, seasonal figures. Empowers mothers, retirees & disabled workers. Ships to 4 continents.

name: Käthe Kruse
description: Germany. Historic German doll maker. 100+ years. Soft fabric collector and play dolls.

name: Dolls 4 Tibet
description: Fair trade Waldorf-style dolls supporting Tibetan communities.

name: Start with the kinder lyre
description: The kinder lyre (also called kinder harp or pentatonic lyre) is the most versatile Waldorf home instrument. It is tuned to the pentatonic scale so everything played on it sounds beautiful — parents don't need to know music to begin. Play it softly at bedtime, during rest time, or to accompany singing. Children aged 2+ can pluck it. The most recommended first instrument for a Waldorf home. Available from Choroi, Auris, Harps of Lorien and many Waldorf suppliers.

name: Sing every day — without apology
description: The most important thing you can do musically for your child is simply sing — even if you think your voice is imperfect. Children do not hear imperfection. They hear love, presence and warmth. Sing the transition songs in this directory. Sing the seasonal songs. Sing the meal blessing. Sing a lullaby. The voice you have is perfect enough.

name: The pentatonic flute (Ages 6+)
description: A Choroi pentatonic flute is the first instrument a Grade 1 Waldorf child receives. It is tuned to the pentatonic scale — only five notes, all harmonious. Children learn to play by imitation, not notation. At home, the parent learns alongside the child. Simple seasonal songs, lullabies and nature melodies can be played within the first few lessons. Available from Choroi.org · Waldorf instrument suppliers · approximately €25–35.

name: Pentatonic glockenspiel (Ages 3+)
description: The Auris pentatonic glockenspiel is a beloved home instrument — six or eight bars tuned to the pentatonic scale, in a beautiful wooden frame. Played with a soft mallet. A child can play it alone without producing discord — every note combination sounds harmonious. Ideal for toddler musical exploration and early childhood free play. Available from Auris (aurisinstruments.com) · Bella Luna Toys · Waldorf suppliers worldwide.

name: Recorder (Ages 9+ / Grade 3)
description: The soprano recorder is the standard Grade 3–8 Waldorf school instrument — affordable, portable, beautiful when well played. Mollenhauer and Moeck are the preferred German wooden recorder makers used in Waldorf schools. Avoid plastic recorders where possible — the wooden tone is warmer and more alive. A good wooden soprano recorder costs approximately €20–40. Lessons at home: the Waldorf recorder songbook series by many publishers.

name: String instruments (Ages 9+ / Grade 3)
description: Most Waldorf schools begin violin or cello in Grade 3. Hiring rather than buying is strongly recommended for the first 1–2 years. Waldorf string education follows a strongly aural, imitative approach — the Suzuki method is compatible and widely used alongside Waldorf pedagogy. Practice 10–15 minutes daily in the early years is far more valuable than occasional long sessions.

name: Singing games and circle time at home
description: The simplest and most complete music practice for young children is the singing game — movement, song, rhythm and social interaction all in one. Books: Singing Games for Families, Schools and Communities (Anna Rainville & Laurie Clark, WECAN); Dancing As We Sing (Nancy Foster, WECAN); Let Us Form a Ring (Nancy Foster, WECAN). These three books contain everything a family needs to bring Waldorf music to life at home.

name: Harps of Lorien — Kinder Lyres (USA)
description: Raphael Weisman has been making kinder lyres for over 20 years. The most trusted North American maker of pentatonic children's lyres — used in partnership with the Christopherus Waldorf homeschool curriculum. High quality, affordable, made with care. harpsoflorien.com

name: Choroi
description: Germany. THE Waldorf instrument maker. Developed with the Goetheanum Medical Section. Workshops employ disabled and disadvantaged workers. Pentatonic flutes (pear/cherry wood, 440Hz/432Hz), lyres, harps, glockenspiels.

name: Auris
description: Sweden. Pentatonic & diatonic glockenspiels, xylophones, children's harps and lyres. Maple and birch. Widely used in Waldorf schools.

name: Mollenhauer
description: Germany. High-quality wooden recorders (soprano, alto, tenor). Beloved in Waldorf upper grades.

name: Moeck
description: Germany. Wooden recorders. Used from Grade 3 onward in Waldorf schools.

name: Hokema
description: Germany. Kalimbas in natural cherry wood. B5, B9, B17 — pentatonic tunings.

name: Bartl
description: Germany. Harmonicas. Widely used in Waldorf lower grades.

name: Stockmar
description: Germany. Beeswax crayons and blocks, watercolour paints. Based on Goethe's colour circle. The school standard worldwide for 60+ years.

name: Lyra
description: Germany. Super Ferby triangular coloured pencils. Waldorf assortment sets. Children's grip-friendly design. Also: Lyra Skin Tone coloured pencil sets — available at Cincinnati Waldorf School store and selected Waldorf retailers.

name: Mercurius
description: Netherlands. Chalk, watercolour pencils, colour giants. 30+ years supplying Waldorf schools.

name: Filana
description: USA. Beeswax crayons. Made in USA. Non-toxic.

name: Natural Earth Paint
description: USA. Truly non-toxic earth pigment paints. Green America certified. Recommended for children with sensitivities.

name: Honeysticks
description: New Zealand. Pure beeswax crayons. NZ-made. Very popular in Waldorf homes.

name: 🇩🇪 HABA — Germany
description: Bad Rodach, Germany. Family-run since 1938. Classic wooden toys, building blocks, board games, soft toys. Waldorf-compatible, beautifully crafted. Available worldwide at habatoys.com and major toy retailers internationally.

name: 🇩🇪 Heidi Hilscher Dolls — Germany
description: Germany. Handmade in the Waldorf doll-making tradition. Highest quality — from dresses to delicate features. Expressions deliberately simple to encourage imagination. Available internationally via Waldorf toy shops and The Wooden Wagon.

name: 🇩🇪 Nanchen Dolls — Germany
description: Germany. Companion brand to Heidi Hilscher. Handmade Waldorf-tradition dolls. Lovingly detailed, imagination-fostering. Available internationally via Waldorf toy shops worldwide.

name: 🇷🇴 Wood Pecker Factory — Romania
description: Bucharest, Romania. Hand-crafted wooden animals, trees, flowers, princesses and knights — similar aesthetic to Ostheimer and Holztiger. Sea animals, woodland, farm, African animals, birds, dinosaurs. Etsy: WoodPeckerFactory

name: 🇺🇦 Waldorf World — Ukraine
description: Dnipro, Ukraine. Stunning needle-felted gnomes, fairies, fairy houses, animals, fruits, vegetables and birthday crowns. Wool with real flourishes — pine cones, moss, snail shells, beading. International shipping. Etsy: WaldorfWorld

name: 🇷🇺 Green Taiga — Russia
description: Novosibirsk, Russia. Waldorf-inspired animals and trees from alder wood. Non-toxic water-based paints, linseed oil and wax. Great character through carving. European and American shipping. Etsy: GreenTaiga

name: Ailefo
description: Denmark. Organic modelling clay. No synthetic materials.

name: Namaki
description: France. Organic face paint for children. Certified organic.

name: ⭐ We Are Colorful — Mudpuppy
description: USA. 18 beautiful wax crayons in skin tones far beyond just peach and brown — the full human spectrum. Housed in a sturdy reusable tin. Ages 3+. Meets CPSIA, ASTM and CE safety standards. Designed by Courtney Ahn. Available at mudpuppy.com, Amazon, and toy retailers worldwide. The tin makes it a wonderful birthday gift. "Celebrate the wonderful range of skin tones and help every child feel represented."

name: Faber-Castell World Colors EcoPencils
description: Germany/USA. 27 coloured pencils including 3 duo-tone pencils giving 6 blendable skin tone shades. Developed with makeup artists for accurate skin tone blending. Made from certified sustainable forestry wood. Highly pigmented, smooth lay-down. Available at fabercastell.com and art supply shops worldwide. Also: Faber-Castell Black Edition — 12 skin tone coloured pencils on dark paper.

name: Lyra Skin Tone Coloured Pencils
description: Germany. Lyra's trusted quality in a skin tone assortment. Available at Cincinnati Waldorf School store (cincinnatiwaldorfschool.org) and selected Waldorf art suppliers. Lyra's Super Ferby pencils have been used in Waldorf schools for decades — the skin tone range extends this trusted quality.

For the widest range, combine Stockmar's natural ochre, caramel, sienna and umber tones. Used in Waldorf schools worldwide for main lesson book portrait work. Available from all Waldorf art suppliers.

name: Derwent Coloursoft Skintones
description: UK. Professional-quality coloured pencil set specifically for skin tone work. Soft, highly blendable core. Beloved by older Waldorf students (Grades 6+) for portrait and figure work in main lesson books. Available at art supply retailers and derwent.com

name: 🖐 Fine motor development
description: Strength and coordination in the small muscles of the hands and fingers directly prepares for writing, instrument playing and all handwork. Fingers that can gesture, tap, weave and point with precision are fingers ready to hold a pencil, knit a stitch or bow a violin string.

name: 🧠 Bilateral brain coordination
description: Most finger games use both hands together — or alternate left and right in sequence — crossing the body's midline. This bilateral coordination connects the brain's two hemispheres and is the same neurological foundation required for reading and writing. Finger games are, in the most literal sense, brain-building.

name: 📖 Language and memory
description: Verse, rhyme, repetition and movement together are the most powerful tools for language acquisition available to the young child. The physical gesture anchors the word in the body — the child who acts out "the spider climbs up the drainpipe" remembers the word "drainpipe" forever. Memory is embodied.

name: 🎵 Rhythm and musicality
description: Coordinating speech with movement develops internal rhythm — the foundation of musicality, mathematics and social synchrony. A child who can keep a steady beat with their fingers while saying a verse is a child whose nervous system is learning to organise time.

name: 🔢 Number sense
description: Counting games and one-to-one correspondence are naturally embedded in finger games — "one little finger, two little fingers..." Long before formal arithmetic, the child's fingers teach them that numbers are real, embodied and reliable.

name: 💛 Loving connection
description: The most important dimension of finger games for the very young child is the intimate human contact — an adult fully present, playing, touching, singing. The hand games in Ellersiek's Giving Love, Bringing Joy are specifically designed as touch games for parent and baby. This loving presence is itself nourishment.

🌊 Transition Songs — For the Rhythmic Waldorf Day

It is a much more joyful experience to sing "This is the way we wash our hands" rather than shouting "Come and wash your hands now!" while your toddler cheekily runs around the house with muddy hands. Keep your transition songs simple enough for children to sing by themselves — you will hear children singing the songs on their own, reminding themselves of the steps to accomplish a job. The best transition songs: short (4–8 lines), rhythmic, action-based and sung to a simple melody the child can join in with immediately.

🧼 Wash, Wash, Wash Your Hands (Traditional Waldorf)
Wash, wash, wash your hands
Make them nice and clean
Wash the germs right down the drain
Make them nice and clean
Sung to the tune of Row, Row, Row Your Boat. Simple, rhythmic, action-based. Children naturally mime the washing motion. Used in Waldorf kindergartens and homes worldwide before meals and after outdoor play.
Ages 2+ · Before meals · After play
🧼 This Is the Way We Wash Our Hands (Traditional)
This is the way we wash our hands
Wash our hands, wash our hands
This is the way we wash our hands
Before we eat our food
Sung to the tune of Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush. Add verses: "This is the way we dry our hands… / This is the way we comb our hair…" — endlessly adaptable for any routine.
Ages 2–6 · Daily routines
🧹 Clean-Up Song — Twinkle Version (Traditional Waldorf)
Twinkle, twinkle little star
Stop and clean up where you are
It's time to put the toys away
We will play another day
Twinkle, twinkle little star
Stop and clean up where you are
Sung to the tune of Twinkle Twinkle Little Star. Gets the job done and offers encouragement of fun the next time the children are together. Warm, reassuring — "we will play another day" honours the child's play rather than simply ending it.
Ages 2–7 · Tidy-up time
🧹 Everybody Clean Up (Traditional)
Everybody clean up, clean up, clean up
Everybody clean up, after lunch
Trash in the trashcan, recycle in the bin
When we work together we all win!
Light, energetic and community-minded — "when we work together we all win" is deeply Waldorf in spirit. Change words to suit context: "clean up after play / clean up before we go."
Ages 3–8 · After meals · Tidy-up
🎒 Getting Ready to Go Outside (Traditional Waldorf)
Put on your snow boots — tug, tug
Put on your winter coat — zip, zip
Put on your cosy hat — whoop!
Put on your mittens now — both hands!
We're playing in the snow, hurray!
Sung to The Farmer in the Dell or another simple tune. The onomatopoeic words (tug, zip, whoop) delight young children and prompt the action simultaneously. Adaptable for any season — "put on your sun hat / put on your raincoat."
Ages 2–6 · Getting dressed · Seasonal
🚶 Walking Down the Hall (Traditional)
We're walking down the hall
We're walking down the hall
Let's keep together, friends
We're walking down the hall
A simple moving verse for transitions between rooms or from indoors to outdoors. The rhythm of the song naturally regulates the pace of children's feet. Change to "We're walking to the garden / We're walking to the table."
Ages 2–7 · Moving transitions
👋 Welcome Song — Each Child Named (Traditional)
We're all here today
We're all here today!
Clap, clap, oh clap your hands
We're all here today!
[Child's name] is here today
Clap, clap, oh clap your hands
[Child's name] is here today!
A favourite for opening circle because clapping keeps everyone involved. Children are invited to dance in the circle after their verse. Every child is named, seen and celebrated. A profound act of recognition for the young child.
Ages 2–7 · Morning circle · Opening
🛏️ Rest Time Verse (Traditional)
The flowers, they grow on your ten little toes
All the way up to your little nose
The petals unfold as you rest and be still
Breathe in the perfume and be, if you will
A therapeutic touch verse for rest time — gentle massage of toes while singing. Can be accompanied by light touch to help the child settle. Particularly beautiful after outdoor play before the midday meal.
Ages 1–5 · Rest time · Therapeutic touch
🍞 Before Baking / Cooking (Traditional Waldorf)
Little hands so busy
Kneading, kneading, kneading
Round and round the dough goes
Warm and soft and growing
Into the oven, into the oven
Warm and golden baking
A simple verse to sing while kneading bread dough — one of the classic Waldorf kindergarten activities. The words follow the action. Children love joining in with the kneading motion.
Ages 3–7 · Baking · Handwork
🌙 Goodbye / End of Day (Traditional Waldorf)
Now we take our love and light
Back to mother smiling bright
Back to father, kind and warm
Holding baby in their arms
Goodbye now, goodbye!
Blessings on our day!
The classic parent-child closing verse. Bridges the child from the group back to the family with warmth and care. The day is not simply "over" — it is consciously returned to the home with a blessing.
All Ages · Closing · Goodbye
💡 How to Create Your Own Transition Songs
description: Choose a familiar tune — Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush, The Farmer in the Dell, Row Row Row Your Boat, are all good choices. Then make up a rhyme — one concept per verse. You will usually need 8 beats to fit into the song — play around with it until your song is satisfying! The best transition songs are personal, specific and sung consistently — the same song, the same tune, every single day. That is what makes them work. Children begin to self-regulate simply upon hearing the opening notes.

name: The Mood of the Fifth
description: Before the pure pentatonic scale, Steiner identified an even earlier musical mood — the "mood of the fifth" — for the very youngest children (ages 0–5). This is an open, floating, unresolved musical quality using the interval of a fifth. It creates a sense of infinite space, like a question hanging in the air without needing an answer. Waldorf lullabies and nursery songs in this mood have a quality of hovering between earth and heaven — perfect for the baby and toddler still arriving into the world. Julius Knierim's Quintenlieder (Mood of the Fifth songs) is the classic resource.

name: Pure Pentatonic
description: From approximately ages 3–7 (Kindergarten through Grade 2), the pentatonic scale is used exclusively. Songs feel open, dreamy, never quite resolved. There are no leading tones pulling toward a final note — the child floats in the music as they float in play. Instruments tuned to the pentatonic scale — kinder harp, pentatonic lyre, glockenspiel — create a harmonious and ethereal sound perfectly suited to young children.

name: Diatonic Scale & Folk Songs
description: Many folk songs are either in the pentatonic scale or in one of the traditional modes — these tonalities are precursors to our more familiar major and minor scales and lend themselves well to improvisation. From Grade 3 onward, the full diatonic scale arrives with the 9-year change. Music now has a clear tonic, a clear ending. The child stands on firm ground musically as they do developmentally.

name: Why no minor key for young children?
description: Young children should not be given songs in minor keys — the sadness, heaviness and earthward pull of minor tonality is too much for the soul of a child still arriving into the world. Minor keys appear in the Waldorf curriculum from Grade 3–4 onward, once the child has established themselves on the earth. Before this, all songs are major-inflected or pentatonic.

name: 🌱 Spring Songs
description: Spring is announced through song weeks before it arrives — the children hear the songs and feel spring coming. Classic spring songs: In the Springtime Little Bunnies Go Hop Hop (circle movement song) · The Farmer is Working the Fields (farming rhythm song, Grade 3) · Humble Bumble Bees Are Buzzing (nature song, variable tempo) · Down by the Station · Spring nature rounds. Seeds, blossoms, bees, birds returning.

name: ☀️ Summer / St. John's Songs
description: Midsummer songs celebrating the sun at its height. Fire songs, songs of warmth and light, outdoor singing. The Sun with Loving Light is especially powerful at Midsummer. Outdoor circle games and singing games are at their richest in June. Water songs for water play.

name: 🍁 Autumn Songs
description: Autumn Leaves Are Falling Down · Put On Your Dresses of Red and Gold · Autumn Good Morning, Summer Good Night · harvest songs, apple picking songs, hedgehog and squirrel preparing for winter. Michaelmas dragon songs for older children. Warm, earthy tones. Songs slow down as the year breathes in.

name: 🕯️ Martinmas Songs — November
description: Lantern songs are among the most beautiful in the Waldorf tradition. Children make paper lanterns and walk in procession after dark. I Go With My Little Lantern (German: Laterne Laterne) is sung in schools across Europe, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. Also: St. Martin sharing his cloak song.

name: 🌟 Advent Songs
description: The Advent garden is accompanied by the most beloved songs of the Waldorf year. Flicker Little Candle · Sunlight Fast is Dwindling · Glimmer Lantern Glimmer · The Earth Was Dark. Songs grow quieter and more inward through the four weeks of Advent, building to the profound stillness of Christmas. The Advent spiral walk is done in silence, broken only by song.

name: ❄️ Winter Songs
description: Snow songs, frost songs, songs of the sleeping earth. Where Are the Froggies When the North Wind Blows? · star songs, animal sleep songs, cozy warmth and hearth songs. The mood is inward, hushed, tender. Winter songs are the most lullaby-like of the year.

name: 🌼 Easter / Spring Festival Songs
description: Resurrection songs, butterfly songs, seed-growing songs. Blessings on the Blossoms · Down by the Station Rainbow Fairies. Easter songs celebrate transformation — the caterpillar becoming a butterfly, the seed becoming a plant — with great joy and light.

name: 🐉 Michaelmas Songs — September
description: Songs of courage, light overcoming darkness, the archangel Michael and the dragon. Michael and the Dragon songs for Grades 3–5. Rowan berry songs, iron songs, harvest songs. Michaelmas songs have a different quality — stronger, more martial, calling the child to courage as the darker half of the year approaches.

description: Sarah Baldwin (WECAN) shares seasonal Waldorf songs and verses on YouTube. A warm, gentle sung resource for parents wanting to hear how songs are sung authentically. Search "Sunday with Sarah Waldorf songs."

description: Lavender's Blue Homeschool. Free guide to Waldorf circle time songs and verses for kindergarten and early grades. Excellent practical explanation of how to build a morning circle. lavendersbluehomeschool.com

name: Read slowly, twice daily
description: Read the verse once in the morning on waking, and once in the evening before sleep. Do not try to analyse or understand it intellectually. Let the images and language wash over you. The meaning will deepen through the week.

name: Memorise it
description: By midweek, try to recall the verse from memory. Saying it quietly to yourself while walking, doing housework or tending the garden brings it deeper into your life. The verse becomes a companion — always available in the inner world.

name: Connect it to what you see
description: The verses are mirrors of the outer world. In late summer you feel the light drawing inward; in deep winter a warmth stirs from within. Notice how the verse speaks to what you observe in nature that week — the length of day, the quality of light, the temperature of the air.

name: The counter verse
description: Steiner marked each verse from Spring-Summer-Autumn (1–26) with a letter of the alphabet and matched them with corresponding verses for Autumn-Winter-Spring (27–52). This pairing reveals a magnificent polarity of opposing forces that influence the soul striving through the seasons, travelling the path of a lemniscate. The verse exactly opposite yours in the year is your "counter verse" — read both together for depth.

name: Northern vs Southern Hemisphere
description: The first verse starts with Easter during the blossoming of Spring in the Northern Hemisphere. Since it is autumn in the Southern Hemisphere, Week 27 may be a more appropriate starting point on Easter Sunday for those in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, South America. The southern verses begin at the autumn/winter quality and mirror north.

name: Share it with children
description: The verses are deep for young children as written — but their essence can be distilled into a morning verse or nature observation for the family. "This week our verse speaks of the light drawing inward — let's notice together how the days are growing shorter." The Calendar connects home and cosmos.

name: Learn the story first, not the words
description: Read the story two or three times until you feel the shape — beginning, middle, turning point and resolution. Know the bones; let the flesh come in the moment. You don't need to memorise word for word.

name: Create a simple ritual
description: Light a candle. Dim the lights. Sit together in the same spot each evening. A short opening verse signals: "now story-time begins." The ritual creates anticipation and a sacred space for the story to enter.

name: Slow down and pause
description: Silence is not emptiness — it is where the child's imagination fills in the pictures. Speak slowly, especially at turning points. Let the dragon appear in silence before you name it.

name: Tell the same story many times
description: Young children especially love repetition. Each time they hear the same story they go deeper into it. Repeat a story for a week, a month, a whole season. It becomes part of them permanently.

name: Use your voice as an instrument
description: Louder for the giant, softer for the fairy, slower for sadness, faster for the chase. You need no costumes or props. Your voice contains all the characters — let it.

name: Where to learn more
description: Storytelling with Children — Nancy Mellon (Hawthorn) · susanperrow.com (therapeutic storytelling) · tiptoes-lightly.net (Reg Down — 230+ free stories by age and grade) · dancinghandsfrolickingvoices.org (Lynn St Pierre)

name: Will forces and the hands
description: In Steiner's developmental view, the will is educated through the hands. Thinking educates itself through study; feeling through art and music; but the will — the capacity to act, to persist, to complete — is built through practical physical work. Woodwork is one of the primary will-educating activities in the Waldorf curriculum, alongside handwork, gardening and eurythmy.

name: Fine motor development and brain development
description: Using the brain to control the hands, tools and natural materials is one of the most complex neurological activities a human being performs. Like handwriting, it stimulates multiple regions of the brain simultaneously. Woodworking builds fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, spatial reasoning, powers of concentration and perseverance with difficult tasks.

name: The beauty of useful things
description: Throughout the woodwork curriculum, the teacher awakens an appreciation for the combination of usefulness and beauty. A spoon must fit the hand. A bowl must hold soup. A chair must bear a person's weight. When children make objects that are truly useful and truly beautiful — both — something profound happens in their relationship to the material world.

name: Respect for materials and the earth
description: Wood comes from a living tree. Each piece has grain, character, history. A child who has spent weeks carving a bowl from a single block of wood will never look at a tree — or a piece of furniture — the same way again. Gaining respect for the source of materials is the first stage a child can take towards developing individual responsibility and resourcefulness.

name: Individuality expressed in form
description: From Grade 6 onward, woodwork projects begin to reflect the individual child's style — the curve of a spoon, the proportion of a bowl, the design of a boat. The material resists and the tool corrects. The child must negotiate between intention and reality. This develops sound judgement and authentic self-expression more effectively than any test.

name: Confidence through completion
description: Every woodwork project begins as a raw block of wood and ends as something beautiful and useful. A child who holds a spoon they have made with their own hands — who has struggled, persisted and completed — carries a confidence that no grade can give. "The confidence and satisfaction that comes from making something by hand" is one of woodwork's most important gifts.

name: Crossing the midline
description: Knitting requires both hands to work in coordinated alternation across the body's midline — a fundamental neurological development skill that connects the right and left hemispheres of the brain. This is required for overall coordination and for everyday tasks such as writing, reading, and dressing. Research confirms what Waldorf education has long practised: fine motor development is directly connected to literacy and numeracy.

name: Educating the will
description: A pair of socks takes the entire school year to complete. A Waldorf doll takes months. Handwork teaches patience, persistence and the capacity to hold a long-term goal in mind through daily practice. This education of the will — the ability to sustain effort toward a distant completion — is one of the most vital capacities a human being can develop, and one of the least taught in modern education.

name: Mathematical thinking in the hands
description: Knitting and crochet are fundamentally mathematical — counting stitches, understanding pattern, working with sequences, recognising symmetry, increasing and decreasing at precise intervals. The practice of carefully observing and analysing stitches is a forerunner for pattern recognition, fundamental to mathematics, especially geometry. Children who knit well tend to be strong mathematicians.

name: The beauty of the useful
description: Every handwork project must be beautiful and useful simultaneously. A knitted flute case must be the right size and must be beautiful. A sewn doll must be structurally sound and must have soul. This cultivates aesthetic discrimination — the capacity to care about quality — which is increasingly rare and increasingly precious.

name: Rhythm and the feeling life
description: The rhythmic movements of knitting — the looping, the interweaving, the regularity of stitch after stitch — work directly on the feeling life of the child. Handwork calms. It centres. It creates a healing, meditative state. Children who struggle with anxiety, restlessness or attention difficulties often find that knitting provides exactly the rhythmic physical anchor they need. Research confirms knitting's measurable benefits for mental health (see Betsan Corkhill's work).

name: Connections across the whole curriculum
description: Handwork is not isolated from the rest of learning — it is woven through it. Knitted toy animals in Grade 1–2 connect to fables and the Animal Kingdom block in Grade 4. Sewing a doll in Grade 6–7 connects to physiology in high school. Machine sewing in Grade 8 connects directly to the Industrial Revolution main lesson block. The handwork curriculum and the main lesson curriculum breathe together.

name: Knitting Needles (bamboo or wooden)
description: Grade 1–2: 5–6mm thick bamboo needles. Grade 3: 4mm. Grade 4+: 3.5–4mm metal or bamboo. Avoid plastic. A Child's Dream · Acorns & Twigs · Waldorfshop EU all carry full sets.

name: Crochet Hooks (bamboo)
description: 5–6mm for beginners using chunky Filges yarn. Grade 4–5 typically begin crochet. Bamboo hooks feel warm in the hand — preferred in Waldorf schools.

name: French Knitting Fork (wooden)
description: The very first knitting tool in Grade 1. Filges wooden knitting fork · Maplerose · A Child's Dream. Simple cord-making — the beginning of all knitting.

name: Loom / Weaving Frame (wooden)
description: Filges square children's weaving frame with comb, rod and shuttle. Grade 2–3 standard. Also: rigid heddle looms for Grade 4–5. Waldorfshop EU · A Child's Dream · Bella Luna Toys.

name: Felting Needles + Foam Pad
description: Coarse needle for attachment work; fine needle for detail. Always use foam pad to protect work surface. Filges · The Felting Source · Living Felt · Weir Crafts all sell good sets.

name: Bubble Wrap + Mesh for Wet Felting
description: Bubble wrap (bumpy side up) + mesh netting + warm soapy water. All standard wet felting tools. Available at hardware stores or through The Felting Source / Living Felt as kits.

name: Embroidery Hoop + Needle
description: For Grade 4+ cross-stitch and embroidery. Wooden hoops only (no plastic). Maplerose · A Child's Dream · Acorns & Twigs carry appropriate sizes and blunt needles for children.

name: Drop Spindle (wooden)
description: For Grade 5–6 spinning introduction. Simplest form of spinning. Weir Crafts · A Child's Dream · Fibrecraft carry lightweight spindles suitable for beginners.

name: 1912 — The First Founding
description: The first Anthroposophical Society was founded in Cologne on 28 December 1912, growing out of Rudolf Steiner's German section of the Theosophical Society after a decisive break over the question of Krishnamurti. Founding members included Marie von Sivers (later von Steiner), Michael Bauer and Carl Unger. The Society was formally constituted at the General Assembly in Berlin, February 1913.

name: 1913–1922 — The First Goetheanum
description: The Goetheanum — designed by Rudolf Steiner down to its last sculptural detail — was built in Dornach, Switzerland as the centre of the anthroposophical movement. Built largely by volunteers from across Europe. New Year's Eve 1922: the first Goetheanum was destroyed by arson. Steiner immediately began designing the second Goetheanum — in concrete — which stands today.

name: 1923 — The Christmas Conference
description: At Christmas 1923 in Dornach, Steiner re-founded the Society as the General Anthroposophical Society — placing himself at its head for the first time and uniting the outer Society with the esoteric School of Spiritual Science. He gave the Foundation Stone Meditation as the spiritual cornerstone. This conference is considered the most significant single event in the history of the anthroposophical movement.

name: 1924–1925 — The Final Year
description: In 1924 alone, Steiner gave the Agriculture Course (biodynamics), the Curative Education Course, the Pastoral Medicine Course, the Art of Education courses, the Karma lectures (over 80 lectures), the First Class of the School of Spiritual Science, and the Calendar of the Soul Supplement verses. He collapsed in September 1924 and died on 30 March 1925. He left behind over 6,000 lectures and 30 written books.

name: Today — A Living Worldwide Movement
description: Today the General Anthroposophical Society connects many hundreds of groups, branches and regional societies worldwide. The spectrum ranges from open discussion meetings to specialised thematic working groups, from spiritual science study groups to informal reading circles, to people from all areas of life committed to inner development and practical service. The Goetheanum in Dornach remains the world centre and hosts an annual General Assembly.

name: Study and reading circles
description: The most common activity — a small group meets regularly (weekly or monthly) to read and discuss Steiner's writings or lectures. Often a single book is read aloud and discussed over many months. The slow, communal reading of a text reveals dimensions invisible to solitary study. Open to newcomers in most groups.

name: Lectures and public events
description: Branches regularly invite speakers to lecture on aspects of anthroposophy, Waldorf education, biodynamic farming, anthroposophic medicine, the arts and social questions. Many events are open to the public and free of charge. Check your national society's events calendar.

name: Seasonal festivals
description: Branches celebrate the four major festivals of the year — Michaelmas (September), Christmas/Advent, Easter and St. John's/Midsummer — with artistic programmes, lectures and community gatherings. These festivals bring together Waldorf teachers, parents, biodynamic farmers, doctors, artists and general members.

name: Artistic activities
description: Many branches maintain ongoing artistic activity — eurythmy groups, speech formation workshops, painting groups, sculpture courses. The arts are understood in anthroposophy not as entertainment but as a path of inner development. Artistic work done in the right spirit can be as spiritually nourishing as meditation.

name: The School of Spiritual Science
description: The esoteric heart of the Society. The First Class (19 foundational lessons given by Steiner in 1924) is conducted by Class Holders in branches worldwide. Attendance at the First Class requires formal Society membership and a year of active participation. The Second and Third Classes were never completed before Steiner's death.

name: Starting a study group
description: You don't need to wait to find an existing group — two or three people reading Steiner together with sincere interest is all that is needed to begin. Contact your national society to register the group and connect with resources. The ASA handbook for groups and branches (free PDF at anthroposophy.org) is an excellent guide.

name: Freie Waldorfschule Uhlandshöhe — Stuttgart
description: The first Waldorf school in the world — founded 7 September 1919. Still operating today at the same address in Stuttgart. The Uhlandshöhe is a hill in Stuttgart's east end. The original school building, designed with Steiner's input, still stands. A living monument to the beginning of a global education movement. waldorfschule-uhlandshoehe.de

name: Emil Molt (1876–1936) — The Founder
description: Director of the Waldorf-Astoria cigarette factory in Stuttgart. Deeply committed to social renewal through education. Approached Rudolf Steiner in 1919 with the vision of a new kind of school for workers' children. Molt provided the building, the funding and the commitment. Without Emil Molt there would have been no first Waldorf school.

name: Karl Stockmeyer (1885–1963)
description: One of the founding teachers of the first Waldorf school. Author of Rudolf Steiner's Curriculum for Waldorf Schools — the definitive curriculum document, compiled from Steiner's faculty meetings and still used as a primary reference by Waldorf schools worldwide.

name: Caroline von Heydebrand (1902–1938)
description: One of the most gifted of the first Waldorf teachers. Author of Childhood: A Study of the Growing Soul — a beautiful and profound account of child development in the Waldorf tradition. Died tragically young. Her work remains one of the most loved books in Waldorf early childhood education.

name: Attend Waldorf school seasonal fairs

name: Morning gathering & circle

name: Morning craft or artistic activity

name: Outdoor free play

name: Lunch & rest

name: Afternoon activity
description: Water play, swimming, nature walk, storytelling, singing games, theatre rehearsal, farm chores, outdoor games, cooking snacks. Theme-specific and age-appropriate.

name: Closing circle

name: Register in January

name: Ask about scholarships

name: Join the waitlist
description: If your preferred session is full, join the waitlist immediately. Waldorf camps often have significant turnover as families' summer plans change — waitlisted families frequently get spots.

name: Open to all children

name: Find your nearest camp

name: Southern Hemisphere timing

name: The farm as a living organism
description: Biodynamic agriculture is an ecological, holistic, and regenerative approach to farming, food, and nutrition. It is founded on a deep respect for nature, and a recognition that everything in our world, above and below, is beautifully interconnected — soil, water, plants, animals, people, and the cosmos. In the ideal biodynamic farm, the whole farm — fields, livestock, woodland, compost, garden — functions as a single self-sustaining organism.

name: Beyond organic
description: Biodynamic goes further than organic. Organic farming avoids harmful inputs; biodynamic farming actively builds life forces in the soil and plant through specific preparations, timing by the cosmic calendar and treatment of the farm as a whole. As one Demeter farmer puts it: "Biodynamics is the oldest, most established holistic farming practice and at the same time the most future-bearing — truly regenerative for soil, planet, economy and human communities. Agriculture 3.0."

name: The biodynamic preparations
description: At the heart of biodynamic practice are eight specific preparations — numbered 500–508 — made from medicinal plants, minerals and animal materials, used in tiny quantities to enliven soil, compost and plants. The most famous are: Preparation 500 (horn manure — cow manure packed into a cow horn and buried over winter, then stirred with water and sprayed on soil to stimulate root growth and soil life) and Preparation 501 (horn silica — ground quartz crystal buried in a cow horn over summer, then stirred and sprayed to enhance photosynthesis and plant quality).

name: The cosmic planting calendar
description: Biodynamic farmers time their planting, cultivation and harvest by a cosmic calendar — the positions of the moon and planets. Root days (moon in earth constellations) are ideal for root vegetable work; flower days (moon in air constellations) for flowers; fruit days (moon in fire constellations) for fruit and seed; leaf days (moon in water constellations) for leafy greens. Maria Thun developed and researched the Biodynamic Sowing and Planting Calendar over 50+ years — still published annually by Floris Books.

name: Cow horns and spiritual science
description: Rudolf Steiner identified the cow as having a special relationship to the cosmos — the cow's horns are understood as organs that reflect and concentrate cosmic forces back into the animal's digestive system. Packing the horn manure and horn silica preparations inside actual cow horns and burying them over winter/summer is not a metaphor — it is a precise spiritual-scientific practice that experienced biodynamic farmers report produces measurable results in soil vitality and plant health.

name: Demeter certification
description: Demeter USA is the only certifier for Biodynamic farms and products in the United States. The entire farm, versus a particular crop, must be certified, and farms are inspected annually. The Demeter mark is the world's highest standard for ecological and ethical farming — and the only one that requires the biodynamic preparations and cosmic calendar. demeter.net

name: The ancient planetary order
description: Ancient astronomers recognised seven celestial bodies visible to the naked eye — the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn. They arranged them in order of their apparent speed across the sky, from slowest to fastest: Saturn · Jupiter · Mars · Sun · Venus · Mercury · Moon. Each planet was assigned to rule one hour of the day, cycling continuously through the seven. The planet ruling the first hour of each day gave that day its name.

name: From Latin to English
description: The Latin names — dies Solis (Sun), dies Lunae (Moon), dies Martis (Mars), dies Mercurii (Mercury), dies Jovis (Jupiter), dies Veneris (Venus), dies Saturni (Saturn) — survive in the Romance languages: dimanche/lundi/mardi/mercredi/jeudi/vendredi/samedi (French). In English, the Norse and Anglo-Saxon peoples substituted their own gods: Tiw (Mars), Woden (Mercury), Thor (Jupiter), Frigg (Venus) — giving us Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. But the cosmic sequence remained exactly the same.

name: Rudolf Steiner and the planetary forces
description: Rudolf Steiner described the seven planets not merely as physical bodies but as bearers of living spiritual forces — each one streaming specific qualities into the earth, human physiology and human soul life. The correspondence between planets, days, metals, plants, organs, colours and grains is not superstition but spiritual science — the recognition that the cosmos and the human being are made of the same substance, breathing together in a sevenfold rhythm.

name: Why it matters for children
description: In Waldorf education, children live in the rhythm of the week without intellectualising it. Oat porridge on Friday. Barley soup on Tuesday. The colour of the day reflected in the classroom's seasonal table, in what the teacher wears, in the quality of the morning circle. Over years, the child absorbs the sevenfold cosmic rhythm into their body and feeling life — a foundation of order, beauty and connection to the living cosmos.

name: The grain of the day
description: The most grounded way to begin. Serve oat porridge on Friday, rice on Monday, barley soup on Tuesday, millet on Wednesday, rye bread on Thursday, corn polenta on Saturday, wheat bread on Sunday. You do not need to follow this rigidly — even occasional awareness of it brings a quality of cosmic rhythm to the family table.

name: The colour of the day
description: In Waldorf kindergartens, the colour of the day is often reflected in what the teacher wears, in the flowers on the nature table, in the silk draped over the seasonal display. At home: a purple cloth on Monday, something red on Tuesday, a yellow candle on Wednesday. Small, beautiful gestures that mark the day's quality without explanation.

name: The quality of the day
description: Each day has an inner quality — Mercury's lightness and communication (Wednesday is a good day for writing and conversation), Venus's beauty and artistry (Friday for making and creating), Mars's will and courage (Tuesday for difficult tasks requiring determination). This is not superstition but a gentle attentiveness to the living qualities of time.

name: The daily rhythm in school
description: In many Waldorf schools, the day of the week shapes the quality of the lessons without announcement. Tuesday main lessons may have a stronger will-activity quality. Friday may have more artistic work. The teacher who is inwardly attuned to the planetary week brings these forces to the children as an unconscious gift — like sunlight that warms without being seen.

name: The Waldorf Path daily splash
description: Every time you open The Waldorf Path, the daily splash screen greets you with the planet, colour and grain of that day. The background colour shifts. This is your daily cosmic compass — a small, free gift of cosmic orientation to begin your day with awareness of the living forces at work in the world.

name: Further reading
description: Rudolf Steiner speaks about the planetary forces and their relationship to human beings in many lecture cycles — particularly: Man in the Light of Occult Physiology and Occult Physiology (GA 128), Spiritual Beings in the Heavenly Bodies and the Kingdoms of Nature (GA 136), and Nutrition (GA anthology). All available free at rsarchive.org.

name: 🥕 Root Vegetables — Head & Nerve-Sense System
description: Root vegetables are said to have a positive effect on nerves and head. Carrots, beets, turnips, parsnips, celeriac — these grow downward into the earth, drawing mineral forces. They nourish clarity of thought, concentration and the nervous system. In Waldorf nutrition, root vegetables are served especially when mental alertness is needed. Carrot in all its forms is particularly valued.

name: 🥬 Leafy Vegetables & Stems — Heart & Rhythmic System
description: Leafy vegetables, salads and cabbage strengthen heart and lungs. Spinach, kale, lettuce, chard, cabbage, herbs — these grow in the middle zone, between root and flower. They nourish the rhythmic system — heart, lungs and circulation. Connected to the feeling life. Salads and leafy greens are the food of balance, rhythm and equanimity.

name: 🍎 Fruits, Seeds & Flowers — Metabolism & Will
description: Fruits and seeds stimulate digestion and metabolism. Apples, berries, tomatoes, cucumbers, squash, nuts — these grow upward toward the sun, filled with warmth and light. They nourish the metabolic-limb system — digestion, warmth, will and activity. Fruit is the food of action, energy and enthusiasm.

name: 🌈 The Balanced Plate
description: In order to achieve a harmonious equilibrium, food from each different segment should be eaten daily. A Waldorf-inspired meal brings root, leaf and fruit to the table together — nourishing the whole human being, not just one aspect. This is the practical application of the threefold principle in the kitchen.

name: The kindergarten snack
description: In most Waldorf kindergartens, snack preparation is a daily activity shared by the children and the teacher — kneading bread dough, spreading butter, cutting fruit, washing vegetables. The snack is always preceded by a meal blessing verse. Typical: whole grain bread with butter and honey, seasonal fruit, vegetable soup, rice porridge, millet with vegetables.

name: The school garden
description: In Waldorf schools worldwide, there is a conscious effort to keep school snacks and meals as natural as possible. Most schools have a garden and encourage the growing of vegetables and the grinding of grain. The school garden is a curriculum feature from Grade 3 onward — children grow, harvest and cook their own food.

name: Bread baking in school
description: Bread baking is one of the most beloved Waldorf classroom activities — children grind grain, mix dough, knead it with their hands, watch it rise, bake it and eat it together. This single activity nourishes body, soul and spirit simultaneously. It appears most naturally in Grade 3 (Old Testament, farming, crafts) but can be done at any grade.

name: No screens at meals
description: Meals in Waldorf homes and schools are always screen-free, often accompanied by conversation, a story or seasonal music. Eating while distracted is understood to reduce the body's ability to receive the food's nourishment — the digestive process begins with attention, gratitude and presence.

name: Block crayons, not sticks
description: Waldorf chalkboard drawings use block chalk (Stockmar or similar) — not thin chalk sticks. The flat side creates broad strokes of colour; the edge creates lines. Teachers blend, layer and build up colour. The result is nothing like a conventional blackboard — it is a luminous, warm, coloured drawing that fills the board with life and light.

name: Seasonal and curriculum-linked
description: The board changes with the seasons, the festivals and the curriculum block. In autumn the board shows forest floors and harvest. In December, a deep blue Advent landscape. In Grade 3, Noah's ark and ancient Hebrew scenes. In Grade 5, the gods of ancient Greece. Every block has its visual world.

name: Drawing in front of the children
description: When a teacher draws the day's image in front of the class — slowly, step by step — something profound happens. Children hold their breath. They watch the process of creation. They see that beauty can be made with effort and courage. This act of drawing is itself a lesson in will, patience and artistic devotion.

name: Main lesson books echo the board
description: After the board drawing is complete, children often recreate an element of it — or their own version — in their main lesson books with beeswax crayons or coloured pencils. The board is the seed; the child's book is the flowering. The two are in constant artistic dialogue throughout the school day.
